query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A brief, controlled low‐temperature annealing step applied immediately after melt‐quenching, at a temperature slightly below the crystallization onset, will enhance both the glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of phosphorus-containing high‐entropy alloys by promoting beneficial atomic rearrangements in the amorphous network.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys produced by conventional melt-quenching that exhibit relatively low thermal stability and a high tendency to crystallize upon subsequent thermal exposure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a short, controlled annealing treatment immediately after melt-quenching, with the annealing temperature set just below the crystallization onset temperature.
generation.conditions: The annealing should be performed under inert atmosphere at a temperature narrowly below the crystallization threshold (e.g., 5–10°C lower) for a short, optimized duration. The intervention is intended for alloys prepared by standard melt-quenching, and its benefits should be evident when compared to otherwise identical samples that do not receive the annealing step.
generation.structural_mediator: An increase in medium-range order and a reconfigured local atomic network within the amorphous structure.
generation.mechanism: The low-temperature annealing is expected to enable controlled atomic rearrangements that lower the free energy of the amorphous state, increasing the energy barrier for crystallization and thereby stabilizing the glassy configuration.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to this post-quench annealing protocol will exhibit a higher onset temperature for crystallization and improved overall stability of the amorphous phase, as evidenced by delayed crystallization peaks in DSC measurements compared to unannealed controls.
generation.baseline: The performance of as-quenched phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed without any post-quench annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only within a narrow temperature window (just below the crystallization onset) and on systems where crystallization kinetics are similar to those in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys. It may not be effective in alloys with substantially different thermal properties or if the annealing temperature deviates significantly from the optimal range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise annealing temperature and time required for optimal performance need to be experimentally determined, and the degree to which atomic rearrangements improve both glass-forming ability and thermal stability may vary with minor changes in alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the identical phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy composition using standard melt-quenching. Subject one set to a brief annealing treatment at a temperature 5–10°C below the crystallization onset temperature, while leaving the control set unannealed. Perform differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) on both sets to analyze the crystallization onset temperature and the overall thermal stability. Complement DSC data with X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy for structural analysis.
measurements: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) to determine crystallization onset temperature and glass transition parameters
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to check for the presence of crystalline phases
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess atomic medium-range order changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature or if they display signs of premature crystallization or deleterious phase separation compared to the unannealed controls, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

frame.system: Phosphorus-containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys that are currently processed into an amorphous (glassy) state by melt quenching.
frame.goal: Enhance both the glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
frame.limitation: The current alloy compositions tend to crystallize too easily upon cooling or subsequent heat treatments, preventing the formation of a stable glass.
constraints: only a single intervention is to be proposed
the intervention must be specified without presupposing its class
the hypothesis must be testable by stating a predicted improvement against an otherwise comparable baseline
the hypothesis should include conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and a potential experiment to falsify it
frame.regime: Processing via conventional melt-quenching followed by isothermal annealing or differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to evaluate crystallization onset and stability; ambient and controlled temperature conditions relevant to thermal analysis.
prior_attempts: Previous work has focused on varying the proportions of phosphorus and other primary alloying elements to optimize the overall composition.

Multi-intervention strategies (e.g., combining compositional changes with processing modifications) have been examined but did not isolate a single, robust change capable of improving both properties simultaneously.

decision.trend: Early efforts aimed at achieving amorphous phosphorus-containing high‐entropy alloys showed that simply tweaking the primary composition or using rapid quenching can produce a glassy state. For example, PMC11642357 demonstrated that extremely high cooling rates (via melt‐spinning) are required to bypass the conventional crystallization observed in slowly cooled alloys. More recent related work in other high‐entropy systems has indicated that controlled thermal treatments—even triggering glass‐to‐glass transitions—can effectively rearrange the amorphous network, thereby increasing thermal stability. This progression shows that while processing (especially rapid cooling) has been successful in forming glasses, the as-quenched structures still suffer from low thermal stability, and a post-processing thermal “tweak” appears promising for curbing crystallization.
decision.unsolved: Even though rapid quenching can secure an amorphous state in phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys, these materials remain prone to crystallization upon subsequent thermal exposure. A single, robust intervention that both enhances the glass‐forming ability during the initial processing and improves the thermal stability of the amorphous phase is still missing.
decision.lever: Introduce a brief, controlled low‐temperature post-quench annealing step just below the crystallization onset temperature
decision.why: This lever builds on the observed benefits of inducing a glass-to-glass transition in high-entropy systems. By carefully tuning the annealing temperature and time, the intervention is expected to trigger atomic rearrangements that enhance medium-range order in the amorphous network, thereby increasing the energy barrier for crystallization without promoting unwanted phase separation. This approach directly addresses the dual challenge of inadequate glass-forming ability and poor thermal stability in phosphorus‐containing alloys.
